title: Rosemary's Baby (film)
wiki_lead:
Rosemary's Baby is a 1968 American supernatural psychological horror film written and directed by Roman Polanski, based on Ira Levin's 1967 novel. It stars Mia Farrow as Rosemary, a newlywed living in Manhattan who becomes pregnant, and begins to suspect that her elderly neighbors are Satanists who have sinister intentions regarding her and her baby. The film's supporting cast includes John Cassavetes, Ruth Gordon, Sidney Blackmer, Maurice Evans, Ralph Bellamy, Patsy Kelly, Angela Dorian, and Charles Grodin in his feature film debut.
Polanksi adapted the film's screenplay from Levin's novel, and the film was produced and partly-funded by William Castle, a producer known primarily for making low-budget horror films. It marked Polanski's first American production. Although the film is set in New York City, the majority of principal photography for Rosemary's Baby took place on soundstages at Paramount Studios in Los Angeles throughout late 1967. 
Rosemary's Baby had its world premiere on June 12, 1968, and went on to become the eighth highest-grossing film at the United States box office that year, grossing over $30 million. It was met with significant critical acclaim and received numerous accolades, including multiple Golden Globe Award nominations and two Academy Award nominations, winning Best Supporting Actress (for Ruth Gordon) and the Golden Globe in the same category. Internationally, Farrow was nominated for the BAFTA Award for Best Leading Actress, while the film won the award for Best Foreign Film from the French Syndicate of Cinema Critics.
Since its release, Rosemary's Baby has been widely regarded as one of the greatest horror films of all time, and in 2014 was selected for preservation in the United States National Film Registry by the Library of Congress as being "culturally, historically, or aesthetically significant." Critics and film scholars in the intervening years have analyzed numerous themes in the film, including paranoia, women's liberation, Catholicism, and the occult. The film was followed by the 1976 television sequel Look What's Happened to Rosemary's Baby, a 2014 miniseries, and a 2024 prequel, Apartment 7A.

Plot
Guy and Rosemary Woodhouse rent a recently vacated apartment in the Bramford, a large Gothic building in Manhattan, after the previous tenant, an elderly woman, fell into a coma and died. Guy and Rosemary ignore their friend Hutch's warning about the Bramford's dark past involving witchcraft and murder. Rosemary meets a young woman, Terry Gionoffrio, a recovering drug addict whom Minnie and Roman Castevet, the Woodhouses' elderly next-door neighbors, took in. Rosemary admires a pendant necklace the Castevets gave to Terry but dislikes its pungent odor. One night, Terry apparently jumps to her death from the Castevets' seventh-floor apartment. grok_lead: Rosemary's Baby is a 1968 American psychological horror film written and directed by Roman Polanski, adapted from Ira Levin's 1967 novel of the same name. The story centers on Rosemary Woodhouse (Mia Farrow), a young New York City housewife whose pregnancy becomes entangled with sinister forces after she and her actor husband Guy (John Cassavetes) move into the Bramford, an ominous apartment building inhabited by eccentric elderly neighbors including the Castevets (Ruth Gordon and Sidney Blackmer). Produced by William Castle and released by Paramount Pictures on June 12, 1968, the film employs subtle dread, unreliable perceptions, and everyday settings to evoke paranoia about medical authority, spousal betrayal, and supernatural conspiracy. Critically praised for its atmospheric tension and Polanski's meticulous pacing, Rosemary's Baby holds an 8.0 rating on IMDb from over 250,000 user votes and 97% approval on Rotten Tomatoes based on 88 reviews. It earned five Academy Award nominations, including Best Supporting Actress for Gordon, whom it won, alongside nods for Best Screenplay and Best Art Direction. Commercially, the film grossed $33.4 million at the domestic box office on a $3.2 million budget, marking a significant return and contributing to the era's shift toward intelligent, character-driven horror over reliance on gore or monsters. Its influence persists in psychological thrillers exploring themes of bodily violation and institutional distrust, though the film's dream sequence depicting Rosemary's drugged assault drew censorship scrutiny in the UK, where 15 seconds were initially cut.
